rulings.restated: Input — Do all five of these tests apply to you? 1. Your spouse died in 2023 or 2024 and you didn't remarry before the end of 2025 (if your spouse died in 2025, answer No). 2. You have a child or stepchild (not a foster child) whom you can claim as a dependent, or could claim as a dependent except that, for 2025, the child had gross income of $5,200 or more, the child filed a joint return, or you could be claimed as a dependent on someone else's return; an adopted child, including a child lawfully placed with you for legal adoption, is always your own child. 3. This child lived in your home for all of 2025, counting temporary absences by you or the child for special circumstances, such as school, vacation, business, medical care, military service or detention in a juvenile facility, as time lived in the home, but only an absence from which it was reasonable to assume the absent person would return and during which you kept up the home; a child born or who died in 2025, or adopted or lawfully placed with you for legal adoption in 2025, lived with you all year if your home was the child's home for the entire time the child was alive, or since the adoption or placement; if the child did not live with you all of 2025 because the child was presumed by law enforcement authorities to have been kidnapped by someone who isn't a member of your family or the child's family, answer No (the kidnapped-child rule of Pub. 501 is outside this tool). 4. You paid over half the cost of keeping up your home (rent, mortgage interest, real estate taxes, insurance on the home, repairs, utilities and food eaten in the home; not clothing, education, medical treatment, vacations, life insurance, transportation, or the value of your own or a household member’s services; amounts paid from a household member’s own funds, such as Social Security, count as paid by them; TANF or similar payments you received and used for the home count as paid by you). 5. You could have filed a joint return with your spouse the year your spouse died, even if you didn't actually do so.

Pub. 501 says 'You may be eligible to file as a qualifying surviving spouse even if the child who qualifies you for this filing status has been kidnapped', so a qualifying filer gets false.
rulings.ruling: Ruling: scope — p501 p. 11, Qualifying Surviving Spouse, Kidnapped child, allows the kidnapped-child exception, which the owner explicitly kept outside this tool (BUG-0273, BUG-0276). rulings.restated: Input — Were you unmarried at the end of 2025, or considered unmarried for head of household? You are considered unmarried if any of these applies. 1. At the end of 2025 you were legally separated under your state's law by a decree of divorce or separate maintenance (if your divorce wasn't final at the end of 2025, an interlocutory decree, you were married). 2. You are married but lived apart from your spouse for the last 6 months of 2025, and all of these apply: you file a separate return from your spouse; you paid over half the cost of keeping up your home for 2025; your home was the main home of your child, stepchild or foster child for more than half of 2025; and you can claim this child as your dependent, or could except that the child's other parent claims the child under the rule for children of divorced or separated parents. Your spouse counts as living in your home during a temporary absence for special circumstances, such as business, medical care, school or military service, if it was reasonable to assume your spouse would return and you kept up the home during the absence. 3. Your spouse was a nonresident alien at any time during 2025 and you did not elect to treat your spouse as a resident alien.
rulings.model: The prompt requires a home that was the child's main home 'for more than half of 2025' but omits the IRS qualifier '(if half or less, see Exception to time lived with you, earlier)', so a child with a qualifying absence, birth, death or placement could produce a wrong No. It also says the other parent 'claims' the child where the IRS says 'can claim the child'.
rulings.ruling: Ruling: finding; i1040gi p. 15, Married persons who live apart: "Your home was the main home of your child, stepchild, or foster child for more than half of 2025 (if half or less, see Exception to time lived with you, earlier)" and "You can claim this child as your dependent or could claim the child except that the child's other parent can claim the child under the rule for Children of divorced or separated parents"; p501 p. 8, Considered Unmarried, test 4, "(See Home of qualifying person, later, for rules applying to a child's birth, death, or temporary absence during the year.)"; i1040gi p. 15, Exception to time lived with you: "If the person is your qualifying child, the child must have lived with you for more than half the part of the year the child was alive" and the adoption and foster-placement rule. The model is right on both points, and both were introduced by BUG-0272, which restated the considered-unmarried rules for the first time. (1) Condition 2 says "for more than half of 2025" and drops the source's pointer to the exceptions, so a married filer living apart whose child was born in August reads the test literally and answers No. (2) It says the other parent "claims" the child where both sources say "can claim" (p501: "only because the noncustodial parent can claim the child"), so a custodial parent who released the claim on Form 8332 to a parent who then did not claim reads No. Either No reaches household.hoh_fails, the only reader with household.hoh_absence. Witness (stage8.hoh.child.ctc, head of household, child age 0, born_died yes, months 12): unmarried yes gives line 12e $23,625, line 16 $14,378, line 19 $2,200, line 24 $12,153; unmarried no refuses lines 12e, 16, 19 and 24 at household.hoh_fails. An over-refusal, never a wrong amount on the tool's own path. The rest of the restatement matches i1040gi pp. 14-15 and p501 pp. 8-9 (see `.transcription/proposed/hhpass/household.findings.md`, F1 and F2, which propose the wording). Completeness household#3 makes point (1) too.
